text: Mark was a Cornish hero. The great romance of Tristan and Iseult tells of a love triangle between that couple and king Mark of Cornwall. When he was presented with a single strand of hair of dazzling gold, Mark decided the woman whose head the hair came from was the world's most beautiful. He would have her for his bride. Discovering that the woman was the Irish princess Iseult, Mark sent his nephew Tristan to bring her to his court. On the journey home, the pair accidentally drank a potent liqueur that had the magical power to make people love until death. Thus bound, Tristan and Iseult could never be happy apart. Tristan dutifully brought his beloved to the man she was to wed. When Iseult could not bear her wedding night, she sent instead her handmaiden Brangien, who pretended to be the queen. The fated couple finally left the court for several years to dwell together. When they returned, Mark took his wife back without complaint. Mark is a shadowy and passive figure compared to the active lovers. He parallels two Celtic heroes whose wives left them for younger men. King Arthur's queen Guinevere preferred the young knight Lancelot. The aging Irish hero Fionn Mac Cumhaill lost his bride Grainne to his underling Diarmait.
objective: Document Mark, the Cornish king of the Tristan and Iseult romance.
